title: What Drama Is and What Makes African Drama Special
summary: The meaning of drama as a composite art, a definition of African drama and the main cultural roots: oral tradition, festivals, music, audience participation and common themes.

p: Drama is a kind of literature written to be performed on a stage by actors. It is a composite art form: it joins literature (the script), performance (acting), visual art (scenery and costume) and often music and dance. Unlike prose, which has a narrator, drama is shown to an audience through dialogue and action.

African drama is drama written by African playwrights that reflects the African outlook, culture and experience. It is not just drama set in Africa; it comes from an African point of view. It grew into a major force in the middle of the twentieth century, during the struggle for independence, as a way of reclaiming African stories and identity.

1. Oral tradition (the most important influence): storytelling (a storyteller or griot addresses an audience, and the plot is often episodic like a folktale); proverbs and sayings (speech is full of traditional wisdom, riddles and proverbs); folktales (many plays adapt trickster stories such as those of Ananse the spider or the tortoise).

2. Festivals and rituals: traditional festivals were 'total theatre', mixing ritual, masquerade, music, story and audience participation. Playwrights such as Wole Soyinka and J. P. Clark borrowed this idea, so their plays are often ceremonial and not strictly realistic. The masquerade (for example Mmanwu in Igbo land, Egungun among the Yoruba) is both human and spirit and links the living, the dead and the unborn.
3. Music, song and dance: they are part of the story, not a break from it. Songs set the mood, give background like a chorus and express feeling. Dance is a language.

4. Audience participation: in traditional performance the line between actors and spectators was thin; the audience sang, answered and joined in. African drama often breaks the 'fourth wall' (the imaginary wall between stage and audience) to speak to the audience.

Clash of cultures: tradition against modernity, African values against European or colonial ones. Social and political criticism: satire of corruption, dictatorship and social ills after independence. History and myth: telling history from an African view and exploring the relation between people and the gods.

A griot (found mainly in West Africa, for example among the Mande peoples) is a traditional poet, musician and keeper of history who tells the stories of families and kingdoms, praises or advises rulers, and passes on knowledge by word of mouth. Many African playwrights treat the storyteller on stage as a modern griot.

activity: Explain why drama is called a composite art. Write two paragraphs on the difference between a Western play you know and African drama. Research the word 'griot' and describe their role.

title: Efua Sutherland and the Anansegoro: Background of The Marriage of Anansewa
summary: The playwright, the Akan storytelling tradition of Anansesem, the new form Sutherland created, and the setting of the play.

p: Efua Sutherland (1924 to 1996) was a Ghanaian playwright, poet and cultural activist, often called one of the mothers of modern African drama. She founded the Ghana Drama Studio, which became a model for creative work in many countries. She tried to join traditional Ghanaian performance with modern theatre.

Anansesem means 'Ananse stories' (spider stories). It is a traditional storytelling session in the Akan tradition built around Ananse the spider, the famous trickster. Features: a master storyteller leads; the audience takes an active part, answering and singing; short songs are sung at key moments to comment on the story or to move between scenes (these songs are called mmoguo or mmomome in the notes and the play, so use the word your teacher uses); and the hero is a trickster: small, greedy and lazy, but he wins by cleverness over stronger people.

Sutherland created a new kind of play which she called Anansegoro ('Ananse play'). It uses the form of an Anansesem session on a modern stage. The Marriage of Anansewa (1975) is the best-known Anansegoro.

Physical: a 'room' in modern Ghana, but not a realistic room; it is a stage. A silent Property Man hands Ananse each prop he needs (a typewriter, a camera), which reminds us that we are in a story-telling world. Time and atmosphere: modern times, when poverty is a real problem. Old and new are mixed: Ananse uses a typewriter and photographs to carry out an old-style marriage trick.
Different editions of the play spell some names differently (for example the names of the chiefs). Use the spellings in your own edition.

activity: Explain in your own words what Anansesem is and what Anansegoro adds. Write two sentences on the role of the Property Man. Research one traditional Ananse story and note how Ananse wins.

title: The Marriage of Anansewa: Act One
summary: The Storyteller, Ananse's poverty and his scheme to 'market' his daughter to four chiefs, and the first gifts.

p: The play opens with the Storyteller who speaks directly to the audience and tells us we are about to share an Anansesem, a story-telling session.
We meet Kweku Ananse and his daughter Anansewa. They are very poor, and Ananse is tired of his 'ragged-clothed poverty'.

Ananse decides to turn his beautiful, educated daughter into a source of wealth. He will not look for one husband but for four. He writes to four rich chiefs at the same time, without telling any of them about the others, and sends each a photograph of Anansewa. He hopes that each will send 'head-money' (money for the bride) and gifts.
Anansewa is training to be a secretary. She types her father's letters and seems to enjoy the game, though she is a little uneasy.

The plan works very well. Messengers and gifts of money, drinks and cloth arrive from several chiefs, including the powerful Chief-Who-Is-Chief. The act ends with Ananse celebrating his wealth and his cleverness.

The play makes fun of the way money and marriage are connected, but it also invites us to admire Ananse's quick mind. Look for the places where the Storyteller turns to the audience and where songs comment on the action.

title: The Marriage of Anansewa: Acts Two and Three
summary: The crisis, the plan of the fake death, the funeral that tests the chiefs and the 'miracle' ending.

p: The plan has worked too well. Gifts pour in, and Ananse even acquires a fashionable friend, Miss Christina (Christie), with his new money. Then a crisis comes: the chiefs are so pleased that they are on their way to claim the bride. If they meet and learn of his trick, he will be disgraced, and they may take back their gifts.

The master trickster invents a more dramatic plan: Anansewa must 'die'. A funeral will bring the marriages to a graceful end. A shocked Anansewa agrees reluctantly, lies on the funeral bed, and Ananse and Christie start the wailing.

sections.h: Act Three: the funeral as a test
p: The whole act takes place at the funeral. The mourners gather, and messengers from the chiefs arrive one by one and are shocked by the news. Ananse listens to their speeches and gifts, which show what their masters are really like. Some of the chiefs send mean messages or ask for their money back. The Chief-Who-Is-Chief sends a message of real sorrow: in death Anansewa is still his wife; he sends rich gifts, promises to pay for the whole funeral and to support Ananse for life.

Ananse publicly shames the other chiefs and declares that only the Chief-Who-Is-Chief was worthy of his daughter. He then performs a 'ritual' and Anansewa 'wakes up' to the joy of the mourners. Ananse has won: he has found a rich and honourable son-in-law. The Storyteller ends the play by celebrating his cleverness.
Study guides differ on small details such as the exact order of the messengers and the names of the chiefs. Follow the order in your edition of the play.

activity: Explain the crisis that forces Ananse to invent a new plan. Describe how the funeral becomes a test for the chiefs. Say who passes the test and how.

title: The Marriage of Anansewa: Characters and Themes
summary: The main characters and the themes of cunning, tradition and modernity, poverty and greed, and the position of women.

p: Kweku Ananse: the protagonist and trickster; greedy, manipulative and selfish, who uses his daughter as 'bait', but also charming, witty and resourceful. The audience admires his cleverness even if we doubt his morals.
Anansewa: his daughter; educated and not simply a victim; she helps with the scheme, obeys her father when she plays dead and shows quick wits. She is a pawn, but a clever one.
The Storyteller: the narrator and guide; he links the play to the Anansesem tradition and speaks to the audience.
Miss Christina (Christie): Ananse's fashionable friend; shallow and materialistic; she stands for the modern life his money buys.
The chiefs: mostly seen through their messengers; most are as greedy as Ananse; only the Chief-Who-Is-Chief is generous and honourable.
1. Cunning as a tool of survival (central theme): the 'small man' beats the 'big men' with his mind, not his strength or money.
2. Tradition against modernity: Ananse uses a traditional storytelling form and the traditional custom of paying bride-price, but also typewriters, photographs and messages.
3. Poverty and greed: poverty drives Ananse's trickery; the play also satirises the greed of the chiefs.
4. The position of women: women are 'marketed' for marriage; Ananse speaks of his daughter as a kind of newly minted currency; she is made into an object for sale.

sections.h: Is Ananse a hero or a villain?
p: Arguments for hero: he outwits powerful men, helps his daughter to a good marriage and entertains us. Arguments for villain: he deceives people, treats his daughter like goods and lies at a funeral. A good answer takes a side and supports it with events. The play invites both reactions.
She obeys, which suggests weakness; yet she is educated, plays her part skilfully and in the end gains a good husband, which suggests quiet strength. Use evidence from the text.

activity: Write a detailed character analysis of Ananse (two paragraphs) and say whether he is a hero or a villain. Say whether Anansewa is weak or strong, with evidence.

title: The Marriage of Anansewa: Style and the Ambiguous Moral
summary: The Anansesem style: storyteller, audience participation, episodes, songs and language; and why the play's moral is deliberately unclear.

p: The play faithfully recreates a storytelling session. The Storyteller opens the play, introduces the people, interrupts the action to address the audience and closes the play. Audience participation: Ananse and the Storyteller break the fourth wall, speak to the audience and make them accomplices in the plot; we find ourselves hoping that Ananse will succeed.

Episodic structure: the play is built in clear short episodes like a folktale (the plan, the gifts, the crisis, the fake death, the funeral test, the miracle). Songs: short songs sung by a chorus or the audience comment on the action, set the mood and move from scene to scene. They are part of the telling and not interruptions. Language: simple, direct and poetic, full of images and proverbs.

sections.h: A moral that is not simple
p: In a simple fable such as 'The Boy Who Cried Wolf', the moral is clear: do not lie. In this trickster tale Ananse is not punished; he wins. The play does not simply say 'do not be greedy' or 'do not lie'. Instead it:
1. celebrates intelligence: cunning and resourcefulness, especially for the poor and powerless;
2. satirises society: it mocks a world in which greed is common, and Ananse uses the chiefs' own greed against them;
3. criticises the marriage market: it shows a custom in which daughters are 'sold' like property, taken to an absurd extreme.
Satire is writing that uses humour, exaggeration and irony to criticise faults in people or society. Sutherland satirises greed, the marriage market and the love of show.
